opus-5.5.text:
I think evolution strategies are massively underrated for this kind of problem. When you want to optimize through an entire RL loop, say meta-learning an objective function or an optimizer, you're dealing with an extremely long computation graph: thousands of inner-loop updates, each depending on the previous one. Backpropagating through that is a nightmare. Memory blows up, and even if you can afford it, the gradients tend to be chaotic. The loss landscape of the outer objective is often very jagged, and the analytic gradient is high-variance or even misleading. You get exploding gradients and you're very sensitive to tiny perturbations early in training.

ES sidesteps a lot of that. You perturb the meta-parameters, run the whole inner loop forward, look at the final performance, and estimate a gradient from the population. That gives you a smoothed version of the objective, which is often exactly what you want in these chaotic landscapes. You only need forward passes, so memory stays constant regardless of horizon length. And it's embarrassingly parallel.

The real enabler recently has been hardware and software. With JAX you can vectorize and JIT-compile the whole RL pipeline, environment and agent together, on the accelerator. Suddenly you can run thousands of RL training runs in parallel on a single GPU, and evaluating a large ES population becomes cheap. That's what made work like learned policy optimization and discovering new RL objectives practical, where we meta-learn parts of the algorithm and they actually generalize to new environments.

It's not a free lunch, of course. ES scales poorly with the dimensionality of what you're optimizing, so you want the meta-parameters to be relatively compact, like a small network parameterizing a drift function or a loss, rather than millions of weights. And the sample cost is real. But for meta-optimizing over a full learning process with a modest number of parameters, I'd argue it's often the most robust tool we have. It's less elegant than exact gradients, but it works in the regime where exact gradients fall apart.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts backpropagating through the unrolled RL loop with perturbing meta-parameters, running the loop forward, and estimating a gradient from population performance.

r002.rationale: It describes ES as effective for meta-optimizing a full learning process and says JAX-enabled hardware made thousands of parallel RL runs practical.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've thought about quite a lot, because on the face of it, evolution strategies look almost embarrassingly crude. You take your parameters, you perturb them with Gaussian noise, you run the whole thing, you look at how well it did, and you nudge in the direction that worked. No gradients, no credit assignment, just black-box search. And for a long time the field treated that as a kind of fallback, something you do when you can't do anything smarter.

But I actually think the interesting question is what you're optimizing through, and that's where ES gets much more compelling. In a lot of our work, we're not trying to optimize a policy directly. We're trying to optimize something that sits upstream of an entire learning process. So think about meta-learning an RL algorithm, or an objective function, or an environment distribution, or the hyperparameters that govern how an agent learns over thousands of updates. If you want to backprop through that, you're backpropagating through an unrolled inner loop that might be millions of steps long. And the moment you try that, you run into two problems. One is memory, which you can partially solve with truncation, but truncation introduces bias, and that bias is not benign. It systematically favors short-horizon behaviour. The second is that the gradients themselves become chaotic. The inner loop is a dynamical system, and tiny changes to the meta-parameters can lead to wildly different trajectories, so the gradient you compute is technically correct but practically useless because it's dominated by this exploding sensitivity.

ES just sidesteps all of that. You don't need the inner loop to be differentiable, you don't need it to be smooth in any formal sense, you just need it to be evaluable. And the Gaussian smoothing you get for free from the perturbations means you're effectively optimizing a smoothed version of the landscape, which in these chaotic regimes is actually what you want. So in the meta-learning setting, I'd argue ES is often not the crude option, it's the correct option. It's the thing that's actually estimating the quantity you care about, which is the long-horizon outcome of the whole learning process, rather than some truncated, biased proxy.

Now, the obvious criticism is sample efficiency. ES scales poorly with the dimensionality of the parameter space, because you're essentially doing finite differences in random directions. And that's true. If you're trying to optimize a hundred-million-parameter policy with ES, you're going to have a bad time compared to a policy-gradient method. But I think that criticism somewhat misses the point in the meta-learning case, because the meta-parameters are typically much lower dimensional than the agent itself. You might be learning a few thousand parameters that define an update rule, and that's very much in the regime where ES works well. And the other thing is that ES is almost perfectly parallelizable. Every perturbation is an independent rollout, so if you have the compute, the wall-clock story is actually quite good. With things like JAX-based environments where you can run thousands of RL training runs on a single accelerator, suddenly the cost of evaluating a population isn't prohibitive anymore, and that's really changed the calculus for us.

There's also a more philosophical point I find quite appealing, which is that ES doesn't impose structure on the inner loop. When you meta-learn with gradients, you're implicitly constrained to inner loops that are differentiable, and that pushes you toward a particular family of algorithms. With ES, your inner loop can have discrete decisions, it can have hard resets, it can have arbitrary non-differentiable logic, and that opens up the design space quite a lot. You can discover things that you wouldn't have been able to express in a differentiable framework.

So my overall assessment is, don't think of ES as the dumb baseline. Think of it as a tool whose weaknesses in direct policy optimization become strengths when you move one level up and start optimizing the learning process itself. The honest caveat is that it's still quite noisy, you need a lot of evaluations, and the variance of the estimator can be a real problem in high dimensions. But for optimizing through an entire RL loop, especially a long one, I'd take a noisy unbiased estimate over a precise biased one almost every time.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts ES’s sample-based, black-box perturbation evaluations with differentiating through a potentially millions-of-steps-long inner RL loop.

r002.rationale: It describes ES as highly parallelizable and explains that thousands of RL training runs on one accelerator can make population evaluation practical, supporting its suitability at hyperscale.

astra-6.text:
I think the attraction is that you can treat the entire reinforcement learning process as a black box. You perturb whatever parameters you want to optimize, run the learning process, and measure how well the resulting agent performs. You don’t have to differentiate through every update or keep the whole computation graph in memory.

But that doesn’t make the credit assignment problem disappear. You’re trying to infer, from a noisy final score, which perturbations improved learning. If each evaluation requires an entire reinforcement learning run, that can be extremely expensive. And the quality of that estimate depends on the dimensionality, the noise in the environment, and how sensitive the outcome is to those perturbations.

So I’d distinguish feasibility from efficiency. Evolution strategies give you a way to do this when differentiation is unavailable or impractical, and they parallelize quite naturally. But where we can exploit the structure of the learning process to get a useful gradient estimate, I’d generally want to use that information. The interesting question is whether the simplicity and robustness of the black-box approach compensate for the amount of computation it needs.

r001.rationale: The response describes perturbing parameters, running the learning process, and scoring the resulting agent as a black-box alternative to differentiating through each update.

r002.rationale: It mentions natural parallelism but does not report that evolution strategies proved particularly well suited to reinforcement learning at hyperscale.

sol-6.1.text:
I think evolution strategies are a very useful baseline, but I’m skeptical of them as a general solution to optimizing through an entire reinforcement learning process. You perturb some parameters, run the learning process, and use the final return to estimate which direction to move. That’s appealing because you don’t need to differentiate through any of the machinery inside the loop.

But you’re throwing away a lot of structure. You reduce this whole learning trajectory to a scalar fitness, and then you have to recover a useful direction from noisy evaluations. If each evaluation requires training an agent, that can become extremely expensive. Parallelism helps with wall-clock time, but it doesn’t remove the sample cost.

What interests me more is whether we can exploit the structure of the learning process to get better gradient estimates. That’s difficult too: differentiating through updates can introduce instability, and there are issues around the dependence of the data distribution on the parameters. So I wouldn’t say evolution strategies are useless. They’re attractive when differentiation is impractical, or when the outer parameter space is small. I’d just want to compare them against methods that use the information available inside the learning loop.

r001.rationale: It describes perturbing parameters, running the learning process, and using final return to estimate an update direction, while noting this avoids differentiating through the loop.

r002.rationale: It does not say evolution strategies proved particularly well suited to reinforcement learning at hyperscale; it instead flags their sample cost and treats them as a useful baseline in limited settings.
